title: How Pizza Works!
summary: Josh and Chuck explore pizza: a casual opening about how much pizza they eat and their favorite local spot Antico Pizza in Atlanta, then a history of pizza from ancient flatbreads and the word "pizza" in Naples (c. 1000 AD and 1738), tomatoes arriving in Italy, the 1889 Queen Margherita legend, Italian immigrants bringing pizza to New York (Lombardi's, 1905) and Chicago, and American chains (Shakey's, Pizza Hut). They cover dough basics (flour, water, yeast, salt, sugar, shortening), the New York water debate, how yeast and proofing work, sauce and cheese order by style, topping preferences and unusual international toppings, the Neapolitan pizza EU protected designation, Chicago deep dish, Sicilian, Greek and California styles, pizza industry stats, the "Ray's" pizzeria name dispute, Domino's and Tom Monaghan trivia, record-setting pizzas, and a live show announcement. Listener mail from Annie tells of a road-trip accident caused by a honking horn. Sign-off includes social media and contact info.

segments.title: Opening banter and Antico Pizza
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck chat about Chuck's cold, how often they eat pizza, and their favorite Atlanta spot, Antico Pizza, including its basil station and phone argument over a cheese pizza.

segments.title: Ancient origins and the word pizza
segments.summary: The hosts trace flatbreads back to Greece and the first use of the word pizza in Naples around 1000 AD, noting that the word's meaning and dating are uncertain.

segments.title: Peasant food and tomatoes arriving in Italy
segments.summary: Pizza spread as cheap peasant food in Naples; tomatoes came from the Americas via the Columbian Exchange, were once thought poisonous, and reached Italy by a roundabout route. The 1738 date for pizza as known today is also discussed.

segments.title: Queen Margherita legend and the first pizzeria
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the first pizzeria in Naples in 1830, the term pizzaiolo, and the legend of Queen Margherita and chef Raffaele Esposito creating the Margherita pizza in 1889 with the colors of the Italian flag.

segments.title: Pizza comes to America
segments.summary: Italian immigrants brought pizza to New York, Chicago and Philadelphia in the late nineteenth century. Lombardi's opened in New York in 1905, and the hosts note Antico in Naples still operates in its original location.

segments.title: American chains: Shakey's and Pizza Hut
segments.summary: After World War II, pizza chains formed. Shakey's is described as the first US pizza chain, and Pizza Hut was founded in Kansas, reportedly named for its hut-shaped building.

segments.title: Dough ingredients: flour, water, yeast, salt, sugar and fat
segments.summary: The hosts explain the core dough ingredients, why high-gluten flour matters for gluten-free pizza, the New York water debate and Mario Batali's comments on oven gestalt and water cloning, and how yeast produces gas to make dough rise.

segments.title: Making and proofing dough
segments.summary: The hosts describe shaping dough by hand, proofing it under wax paper until it doubles, retarding it in the fridge for about twelve hours, and how sugar affects fermentation and browning. Shortening and oil are discussed as well.

segments.title: Sauce, cheese, toppings and white pizza
segments.summary: The hosts discuss sauce and cheese order by style, white pizza with garlic butter sauce, and their personal topping preferences including sausage, black olives, pineapple, and seasoning on pizza.

segments.title: Chicago deep dish and New York style
segments.summary: They contrast New York pizza built from dough up with Chicago deep dish, where the cheese goes on the dough and the sauce is on top, and note that pizza fans are passionate about their styles.

segments.title: Pizza ovens and the peel
segments.summary: The hosts discuss pizza peels and oven types including electric, conveyor and brick wood-fired ovens, and mention Antico's ovens possibly brought from Naples.

segments.title: Neapolitan pizza and EU protection
segments.summary: Neapolitan pizza is described as thin and bubbly, with a limited diameter and crust thickness, and it received EU regional protection in December 2009, which requires wood-fired ovens and San Marzano tomatoes among other standards.

segments.title: Regional and specialty styles
segments.summary: The hosts list California pizza, Greek pizza in a pan, and Sicilian pizza, including American and Italian versions, and joke about stuffed crust.

segments.title: International toppings and US pizza statistics
segments.summary: They describe unusual toppings from Russia, Japan, India, Brazil and Costa Rica, and state that chicken has overtaken pepperoni as the top US topping. They also cite about three billion pizzas sold yearly and the average American eating forty-six slices.

segments.title: Ray's Pizza name and the pizza trademark
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the many New York pizzerias using the name Ray's, the origin story of Ralph Cuomo's nickname, and three Ray's owners who trademarked the name.

segments.title: Chain pizza trivia and record pizzas
segments.summary: The hosts discuss urban legends about Domino's delivery and its thirty-minute guarantee, Tom Monaghan's politics and planned Catholic town, the expensive Guinness pizzas, the largest pizza in Havana, Florida, and the longest delivery from London to Melbourne.

segments.title: Live show and trivia night announcement
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck announce a live podcast at Comic Con in New York on October 12 and a trivia night at the Cutting Room afterward.

segments.title: Listener mail: Accidents
segments.summary: Annie writes about a family road trip where her brother honked the horn during a Stuff You Should Know segment, causing an elderly driver to brake suddenly and a rear-end collision with no injuries.

segments.title: Sign-off and contact info
segments.summary: The hosts ask for listener stories and pizza info, share Twitter and Facebook details, and give the email address and website for more.
